functional.text: Schedule a job: one-off at a time (or after a delay) or recurring with a cron expression, with a handler and payload; pause, edit or cancel it.
Execute each job at its scheduled time on a pool of workers.
Retry failed runs with backoff up to a max number of attempts, then dead-letter them.
Show status and history of every run (queued, running, succeeded, failed) for 30 days.

non_functional.text: Timing: a run starts within 2 s of its scheduled time (p99), including top-of-the-hour spikes of ~10×.
At-least-once execution: no run is ever lost when a scheduler or executor dies; duplicates are made harmless with idempotency.
Scale and availability: 100M runs/day, 50M job definitions, no single point of failure.
Job definitions are durable and edits are consistent with dispatch.

assumptions.text: Runs last 30 s on average and up to 1 hour; the scheduler triggers handlers but does not host code.
Many cron jobs are set to :00, so the start of each hour sees ~10× the average rate.

out_of_scope.text: Workflow DAGs with dependencies (Airflow-style), code packaging and sandboxing.

api.request: name, schedule (cron | run_at | delay), handler, payload, retry_policy, timeout; Idempotency-Key
api.notes: next_run_at is computed from the cron expression in the job's time zone.
Already enqueued runs check the job's state before executing.

api.response: [{run_id, scheduled_at, attempt, status, started_at, finished_at, error}]

data.name: jobs
data.fields: job_id PK, owner, schedule (cron | run_at), next_run_at, handler, payload, retry_policy, timeout, status, version
data.why: Partitioned by hash(job_id); index on next_run_at for the due query; transactions to claim and advance.

data.name: job_runs
data.fields: run_id (job_id + scheduled_at), job_id, attempt, status, started_at, finished_at, error, executor
data.why: 100M rows/day, write-heavy, read by job_id; TTL 30 days.

data.name: partition_leases
data.why: Exactly one active scheduler per partition; fails over when the lease expires.

deep_dives.title: Duplicate runs and idempotency

options.name: Trust the queue to deliver once
options.cons: visibility timeouts and scheduler failovers both produce duplicates

options.name: Deterministic run_id = job_id + scheduled_at as the idempotency key, conditional status updates
options.pros: duplicates become no-ops in the handler and in job_runs

deep_dives.choice: Deterministic run_id passed as the Idempotency-Key; job_runs moves status only from the expected attempt (conditional write)
deep_dives.why: At-least-once is the only achievable guarantee, so duplicates must be cheap. Deriving the key from the schedule means even a second scheduler enqueuing the same occurrence produces the same key.

deep_dives.title: Top-of-the-hour spikes

options.name: Claim a few seconds ahead, queue absorbs the burst, add per-job jitter for jobs that allow it
options.pros: smooths the spike; executors autoscale on queue depth
options.cons: jobs that allow jitter start up to N s late

deep_dives.choice: Claim 5 s ahead, let the run queue absorb the burst, autoscale executors on queue depth, and offer an opt-in jitter window for cron jobs
deep_dives.why: Most ':00' jobs don't need second precision; spreading them over a minute turns a 10× spike into ~1.5×, while strict jobs still start on time from the pre-claimed queue.

wrapup.bottlenecks: The jobs store's write load (every run advances next_run_at), the per-partition polling at top-of-the-hour, and slow handlers occupying executor slots.
wrapup.failures: Scheduler dies: its partition lease expires in ~10 s and another scheduler takes over; claimed-but-unenqueued rows roll back with the transaction. Executor dies: the visibility timeout returns the run to the queue. Handler down: backoff, then DLQ.
wrapup.monitoring: Schedule lag (actual start − scheduled_at) p99, due-but-unclaimed rows per partition, queue depth and age, executor utilisation, retry and DLQ rates, and lease handovers.
wrapup.scale: 10×: more logical partitions (rebalance leases), more SQL shards, a sharded queue, and executors autoscaled on queue depth.
wrapup.future: DAG dependencies (run B after A succeeds), per-tenant quotas and priorities, and calendars and time-zone-aware schedules.

parts.title: Job definitions and the schedule store
parts.problem: Durably store 50M job definitions (one-off and cron), keep each job's next_run_at correct, and make edits, pauses and cancels consistent with jobs that are about to be dispatched.

options.name: Key-value store keyed by job_id
options.cons: no efficient 'what is due next' query; a secondary index on time is a hot partition

options.name: SQL partitioned by hash(job_id), B-tree index on next_run_at per partition
options.pros: range query on due time, transactions to claim and advance atomically
options.cons: must partition to scale; the index is written on every run

parts.choice: Postgres partitioned by hash(job_id) into ~64 logical partitions, each with an index on (next_run_at) WHERE active; the API computes next_run_at from the cron expression on create and update
parts.why: 50M rows × ~1 KB ≈ 50 GB fits a handful of SQL shards, and the scheduler needs exactly what SQL is good at: an indexed range query plus a transaction that claims a job and advances its next run together.

parts.title: Finding due jobs without a full scan
parts.problem: Every second, find the jobs whose time has come among 50M definitions and dispatch them within 2 s, including top-of-the-hour spikes of ~10× (≈12k due jobs/s), with no single scheduler box.

options.name: One cron box scanning the whole table every second
options.cons: O(50M) per tick; a single point of failure

options.name: Indexed range query per partition, each partition owned by one scheduler via a lease
options.pros: reads only due rows; scale by adding partitions; failover by lease expiry
options.cons: polling cost per partition; lease handover gap of a few seconds

options.name: In-memory priority queue / Redis sorted set (score = run_at) loaded from the store
options.cons: a second copy of the truth to keep in sync; memory and durability concerns

options.name: Time-bucketed table (one row set per minute) loaded into a timer wheel
options.pros: O(due) reads, great for huge one-off volumes
options.cons: more moving parts; cron jobs must be re-bucketed each run

parts.choice: Each partition is leased (etcd) by one scheduler, which every second claims SELECT … WHERE next_run_at <= now() + 5 s ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 1000 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, enqueues a run and advances next_run_at in the same transaction
parts.why: The index turns 'what is due' into a range read of only the due rows (~12k/s at peak across 64 partitions ≈ 200 per partition per second). Leases give exactly one active scheduler per partition and automatic failover; claiming and advancing in one transaction means a crash never loses or double-advances a run.

parts.title: Dispatch and execution: at-least-once with leases
parts.problem: Hand each due run to one of hundreds of executors, survive executor crashes mid-run without losing the run, and keep duplicates harmless.

options.name: Scheduler calls the handler directly
options.cons: slow jobs block scheduling; a scheduler crash loses in-flight runs

options.name: Queue with visibility timeout; executors pull, heartbeat to extend, delete on success
options.pros: a crashed executor's run reappears automatically; executors scale independently
options.cons: at-least-once: a slow executor can lose its lease and the run executes twice

options.name: Exactly-once via distributed transactions with the handler
options.cons: handlers are external; side effects can't join a transaction

parts.choice: Run queue with visibility timeout: executors pull, extend the lease with heartbeats for long jobs, call the handler with Idempotency-Key = run_id (job_id + scheduled_at) and record status with a conditional update on attempt
parts.why: Exactly-once execution is impossible end to end, so the design picks at-least-once delivery plus an idempotency key that turns duplicates into no-ops. Visibility timeouts make crash recovery automatic with no reaper to run.

parts.title: Retries, dead letters and status visibility
parts.problem: Retry failed runs without hammering a broken dependency, stop retrying poison jobs, and let owners see the status and history of every run.

options.name: Retry immediately in the executor
options.cons: hammers a failing dependency; ties up executor slots

options.name: Infinite retries
options.cons: poison jobs loop forever and crowd out healthy ones

options.name: Reschedule with exponential backoff + jitter, dead-letter after max attempts
options.pros: failing dependencies get room; poison jobs are parked for humans
options.cons: a delay before recovery; needs a DLQ workflow

parts.choice: On failure the executor sets next_run_at = now + base × 2^attempt ± jitter in the jobs store; after max attempts the run goes to a dead-letter queue, an owner is alerted and can redrive it; every attempt is written to job_runs, which the API reads
parts.why: Reusing next_run_at means retries flow through the same due-job path with no second timer system, jitter spreads retry storms, and the DLQ bounds the damage of a bad job. A runs table with a 30-day TTL answers 'did my job run?' without touching the schedule store.
